about: Doctrine nodes for the legal graph. Hand-curated, not derived.
why_curated: Every judgement in the corpus already carries a `subject` that names the
principle it turns on, so the nodes themselves are close to free. The
lineage between them is not: saying that one case refined another is an
interpretive claim, and a model asked to infer it will produce plausible
edges that are wrong. Each edge below is one a lawyer would state without
hesitation, and nothing further is asserted.
There are deliberately no `overruled_by` or `still_good_law` fields.
Precedential status is the highest-value and highest-harm thing this file
could carry, and it is not something to infer or to freeze into a JSON
file that ages. Where a line of authority is genuinely split, the doctrine
is marked `contested` and both sides are named, without either being

edge_meanings.established_by: The judgement the principle is attributed to.
edge_meanings.refined_by: Later judgements that applied, narrowed or elaborated it, in date order.
edge_meanings.contested: There are competing lines of authority; see `contest_note`.

doctrines.name: Rarest of rare
doctrines.summary: The death sentence is reserved for the rarest of rare cases, where the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed, and aggravating and mitigating circumstances must both be weighed.

doctrines.name: Anticipatory bail
doctrines.summary: The power to grant bail in anticipation of arrest is not to be read narrowly, is not confined to exceptional cases, and an order granting it is not ordinarily limited in time.

doctrines.name: Bail is the rule, jail the exception
doctrines.summary: Pre-trial detention is not punishment; the personal liberty of an accused presumed innocent is the starting point, and refusal of bail requires reasons.

doctrines.name: Arrest must be justified, not routine
doctrines.summary: The power to arrest is distinct from the justification for exercising it; an officer must record reasons, and arrest is not automatic on the existence of a cognizable offence.

doctrines.name: Custodial safeguards
doctrines.summary: Requirements attaching to a person in police custody: identification of the arresting officers, a memo of arrest, information to a relative or friend, medical examination, and specific protections for women.

doctrines.name: Registration of an FIR is mandatory
doctrines.summary: Where information discloses a cognizable offence, registration of a first information report is mandatory and no preliminary inquiry is permissible, subject to the limited categories the judgement itself identifies.

doctrines.name: Quashing of criminal proceedings
doctrines.summary: The categories in which the inherent power of the High Court may be exercised to quash an FIR or a proceeding, including where the allegations do not make out an offence or the proceeding is manifestly mala fide.

doctrines.name: Speedy trial and prolonged undertrial detention
doctrines.summary: A speedy trial is part of the guarantee of personal liberty, and detention as an undertrial that has outrun the trial itself is a ground for release.

doctrines.name: Statutory twin conditions on bail
doctrines.summary: Special statutes impose twin conditions before bail may be granted -- that the court be satisfied the accused is not guilty and will not offend again. Whether, and on what terms, such a bar survives constitutional scrutiny has been answered differently in different cases.
doctrines.contest_note: Nikesh Tarachand Shah struck down the twin conditions then in force under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act; Vijay Madanlal Choudhary considered the provision as later amended and reached a different conclusion; K.A. Najeeb held that a statutory bar does not displace the constitutional court's power where trial has been inordinately delayed. A question about a statutory bail bar has more than one answer in the authorities and must not be given one.

doctrines.name: Certificate for electronic records
doctrines.summary: An electronic record produced from a computer is admissible only with the statutory certificate, which is a condition precedent rather than a formality.

doctrines.name: Circumstantial evidence: the five golden principles
doctrines.summary: A conviction on circumstantial evidence requires that the circumstances be fully established, be consistent only with guilt, be conclusive in nature, exclude every other hypothesis, and form a complete chain.

doctrines.name: Right against self-incrimination
doctrines.summary: The protection against being compelled to be a witness against oneself extends beyond the courtroom to interrogation, and covers involuntary administration of narcoanalysis, polygraph and brain-mapping techniques.

doctrines.name: Procedure established by law must be fair, just and reasonable
doctrines.summary: A law depriving a person of life or personal liberty must lay down a procedure that is fair, just and reasonable, not arbitrary or oppressive. The foundation on which most of the criminal-procedure doctrine in this corpus rests.

doctrines.name: Privacy as a fundamental right
doctrines.summary: Privacy is a fundamental right intrinsic to life and personal liberty; a restriction on it must satisfy legality, necessity and proportionality.

doctrines.name: Free speech, vagueness and overbreadth
doctrines.summary: A penal restriction on speech that is vague or overbroad chills protected expression and cannot stand; incitement is distinguished from advocacy and from discussion.

doctrines.name: Sedition confined to incitement to violence
doctrines.summary: Words critical of the government are punishable only where they incite violence or public disorder; strong criticism alone is not an offence.
doctrines.contest_note: Kedar Nath Singh read down the sedition provision then in force. BNS 152 is a differently worded provision, not a re-enactment of it, and how far the reading-down carries across to the new section has not been settled by this corpus. Treat any answer about the reach of BNS 152 as open.
